Description: Kopper's Chewco role required the Chairman/CEO's determination under the Code of Conduct. The Committee saw no evidence it was disclosed to or approved by Lay or the Board.

Description: Kopper receives $2 million in 'management' and other fees relating to Chewco. The Committee could not identify how the payments were determined or what he did to justify them.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron repurchases Chewco's JEDI interest on terms Kopper apparently negotiated with Fastow, while Kopper held undisclosed interests with Fastow in LJM1 and LJM2. Kopper (and a friend to whom he transferred part of his interest) receive more than $10 million on a $125,000 investment made in 1997.
Direct_Quote: Kopper had invested $125,000 in Chewco in 1997. The repurchase resulted in Kopper's ... receiving more than $10 million from Enron.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: With Board approval, Enron enters business relationships with two partnerships managed and invested in by Fastow. The LJM transactions raise Enron's reported results by more than $1 billion and enrich Fastow and co-investors by tens of millions.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Powers and Troubh conclude the Board's decision to allow Fastow's participation was 'fundamentally flawed.' Winokur, a Board and Finance Committee member during the period, is recused from Board-evaluation portions.
Direct_Quote: A relationship with the most senior financial officer of a public company ... should not have been undertaken in the first place.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Other_Parties_or_Subject: Richard Causey (CAO); Richard Buy (CRO); Jeffrey Skilling
Description: The Board required review and approval of all LJM transactions by Causey and Buy, later Skilling, and annual Audit and Compliance Committee review. The Committee finds these controls were not rigorous and were poorly implemented: Causey and Buy read their roles narrowly, and Skilling was 'almost entirely uninvolved' despite representations to the Board.
Direct_Quote: Skilling appears to have been almost entirely uninvolved in the process, notwithstanding representations made to the Board that he had undertaken a significant role.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Despite a required Compensation Committee review, neither the Board nor Senior Management asked Fastow for his LJM compensation until October 2001, after media reports.
Direct_Quote: neither the Board nor Senior Management asked Fastow for the amount of his LJM-related compensation until October 2001

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron enters into more than 20 distinct transactions with the LJM partnerships, of two types: asset sales and purported 'hedging' transactions. Asset sales often occurred near the end of reporting periods.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Near the end of Q3 and Q4 1999, Enron sells interests in seven assets to LJM1/LJM2. Enron later buys back five of the seven, sometimes within months, and LJM profits on every deal. Fastow told the Finance Committee these generated $229 million of 'earnings' in 2H 1999, against reported earnings of $570M pre-tax / $549M after-tax. There is evidence Enron agreed in advance to protect LJM against loss in three deals.
Direct_Quote: Enron bought back five of the seven assets after the close of the financial reporting period ... the LJM partnerships made a profit on every transaction

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron's first 'hedging' deal with LJM, approved by the Board with Fastow's LJM1 participation: Enron transfers its own stock to an SPE for a note, with LJM1 supplying outside equity, so the SPE purports to absorb declines in Enron's Rhythms stock investment. Enron's own stock is the principal source of payment.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The 'Raptor' vehicles, funded principally with Enron stock or contracts for it, purport to hedge a large group of merchant investments. LJM2 provides the outside equity.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron recognizes $95 million after-tax income from Rhythms in 1999. In the last two quarters of 2000 it recognizes $500 million of derivative revenues from the Raptors and $532 million of pre-tax earnings, more than 80% of its $650 million reported pre-tax earnings for that period.
Direct_Quote: 'Earnings' from the Raptors accounted for more than 80% of that total.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Two Raptors lack credit capacity to pay Enron. In late March 2001 Enron faces a pre-tax charge of more than $500 million.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Rather than take the loss, Enron 'restructures' the Raptors, including transferring more than $800 million of contracts to receive its own stock just before quarter-end. This was apparently not disclosed to or authorized by the Board, gave very substantial value for insufficient consideration, and 'continued the concealment' of merchant-investment losses.
Direct_Quote: Rather than take that loss, Enron 'restructured' the Raptor vehicles

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Raptor SPEs are terminated in September 2001, producing the October 16 $544 million after-tax charge and $1.2 billion equity reduction. Enron had been 'hedging' its investments 'not with a creditworthy counter-party, but with itself.'
Direct_Quote: the charge against earnings was the result of Enron's 'hedging' its investments—not with a creditworthy counter-party, but with itself.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: In recent Congressional testimony, Andersen's CEO says the firm was simply wrong in 1999 to conclude the LJM1 Rhythms SPE met non-consolidation requirements.
Direct_Quote: the firm had simply been wrong in 1999

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron announces retroactive consolidation of the LJM1 SPE to 1999, cutting net income by $95 million in 1999 (of $893M) and $8 million in 2000 (of $979M).

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Andrew Fastow; Michael Kopper; four other Enron employees
Description: Fastow offers interests in the Rhythms termination to Kopper and four other employees through 'Southampton Place.' Fastow's family foundation turns $25,000 into $4.5 million in about two months, and two employees who each invested $5,800 each receive $1 million. No Code of Conduct clearance is found.
Direct_Quote: In exchange for a $25,000 investment, Fastow received (through a family foundation) $4.5 million in approximately two months.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Enron; Enron Global Finance; Vinson & Elkins; Andersen
Description: Enron's public disclosures of the LJM deals were 'obtuse' and did not convey their substance or Fastow's financial interest. This resulted from an effort to avoid disclosing his interest and to downplay and 'disguise' the deals, and the 'reasonable compared to third parties' assertion apparently had no factual basis.
Direct_Quote: these disclosures were obtuse, did not communicate the essence of the transactions completely or clearly

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Fastow was on both sides of the deals. He put his and LJM's interests ahead of Enron's, used his position to influence Enron negotiators, and failed to disclose Kopper's role in Chewco/LJM2 and the LJM partnerships' profitability to the Board.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: As CEO, 'in effect, the captain of the ship,' Lay bears ultimate responsibility. He approved the Fastow arrangements, the Rhythms deal and three Raptors, and did not direct attention to LJM oversight.
Direct_Quote: Lay was the Chief Executive Officer of Enron and, in effect, the captain of the ship.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Skilling personally supported Fastow's LJM participation and had direct responsibility for controls. He described his assigned oversight role as minimal, which 'misses the point.' He 'certainly knew or should have known' the magnitude and risks and bears substantial responsibility.
Direct_Quote: Skilling certainly knew or should have known of the magnitude and the risks associated with these transactions.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: McMahon meets Skilling and raises serious concerns about LJM dealings and Fastow pressuring Enron negotiators. The two disagree on what was said. If McMahon's account (with talking points) is right, Skilling took no action, and McMahon did not approach Lay or the Board.
Direct_Quote: McMahon told us that he approached Skilling with serious concerns about Enron's dealings with the LJM partnerships.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Although Skilling denies it, other employees' accounts suggest he approved the March 2001 Raptor restructuring designed to conceal losses and withheld information from the Board.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Causey presided over accounting judgments that went 'well beyond the aggressive,' mostly with Andersen's concurrence. He did not identify all LJM transactions or give full Raptor III/restructuring information to the Audit Committee.
Direct_Quote: went well beyond the aggressive

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Buy did not implement a procedure to identify all LJM transactions and saw his role more narrowly than the Board believed.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Board 'failed ... in its oversight duties.' It underestimated the conflict, failed to demand and probe information, and authorized Rhythms and three Raptors that many members did not understand.
Direct_Quote: the Board of Directors failed, in our judgment, in its oversight duties.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Finance Committee was told in May 2000 that a proposed Raptor deal raised a risk of 'accounting scrutiny,' and also that Andersen was 'comfortable' with it.
Direct_Quote: accounting scrutiny ... comfortable

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Compensation Committee did not review Fastow's LJM compensation as assigned, even after notice that LJM deals were contributing very large percentages of earnings.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Andersen did not fulfill its audit responsibilities, admitted error on Rhythms, structured the Raptors (charging over $1 million) without objective judgment, and allegedly approved the March 2001 equity recording.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: In September 2001 Andersen requires Enron to reverse the equity accounting from the Raptor restructuring, leading to the $1.2 billion equity reduction.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Arthur Andersen partners; Andersen engagement partner
Description: An internal Andersen e-mail from February 2001 shows concerns about related-party disclosure. A week later, Andersen's engagement partner tells the Audit Committee 'required disclosure [had been] reviewed for adequacy' and that it would issue an unqualified opinion.
Direct_Quote: [r]equired disclosure [had been] reviewed for adequacy

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: From 1997 to 2001 Enron pays Andersen $5.7 million specifically for LJM and Chewco work.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: V&E advised on structures and drafted disclosures. It should have brought 'a stronger, more objective and more critical voice' to the disclosure process. (These portions reflect only Troubh and Winokur, because of Powers's UT Law ties to V&E.)
Direct_Quote: Vinson & Elkins should have brought a stronger, more objective and more critical voice to the disclosure process.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Kopper enriched himself through Chewco, Southampton and possibly LJM2, violated the Code of Conduct, and secretly offered a Southampton interest to another employee.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Ben F. Glisan, Jr. (accountant; later Treasurer)
Description: Glisan was the principal hands-on Enron participant in Chewco and the Raptors. There is substantial evidence he knew the facts showing Chewco failed non-consolidation, and he shares responsibility for Raptor accounting that went 'well beyond the aggressive.' He violated the Code of Conduct by taking a Southampton Place interest without disclosure while working on LJM2 deals.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Kristina Mordaunt (in-house lawyer); Kathy Lynn (Finance); Anne Yaeger Patel (Finance)
Description: These three appear to have violated the Code of Conduct by accepting Southampton Place interests without the Chairman/CEO's consent.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Committee concludes the 'tragic consequences' resulted from 'a flawed idea, self-enrichment by employees, inadequately-designed controls, poor implementation, inattentive oversight, simple (and not-so-simple) accounting mistakes, and overreaching in a culture that appears to have encouraged pushing the limits,' and that many could and should have been avoided.
Direct_Quote: overreaching in a culture that appears to have encouraged pushing the limits

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Committee issues the Report 'without further delay' because of the Board's desire for a prompt explanation and 'pressing requests from governmental authorities.'

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Other_Parties_or_Subject: The New Power Company; broadband/technology investments
Description: Enron's Q3 2001 earnings release includes a $544 million after-tax charge 'related to losses associated with certain investments, principally Enron's interest in The New Power Company; broadband and technology investments, and early termination ... of certain structured finance arrangements with a previously disclosed entity.'
Direct_Quote: related to losses associated with certain investments, principally Enron's interest in The New Power Company; broadband and technology investments, and early termination during the third quarter of certain structured finance arrangements with a previously disclosed entity.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: On the analyst call, Lay says shareholders' equity is being reduced by $1.2 billion in connection with 'the early termination' of 'certain structured finance arrangements with a previously disclosed entity' (LJM2).
Direct_Quote: the early termination ... certain structured finance arrangements with a previously disclosed entity.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Report describes the reaction of investors and the media as 'intense and negative.'
Direct_Quote: The immediate response from the investment community and the media was intense and negative.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron announces the SEC has requested that it voluntarily provide information on the LJM2 related-party transactions.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron announces that Fastow will go on leave of absence and be replaced as CFO.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Board establishes a Special Committee of three non-employee directors to investigate the related-party transactions that are the subject of the SEC inquiry.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Other_Parties_or_Subject: William C. Powers, Jr.; Raymond S. Troubh
Description: Powers (Dean, UT Law School) and Troubh join the Board and the Committee, with Powers as Chairman. Two earlier-appointed directors step down so the new directors form a majority. Final members: Powers, Troubh and Winokur.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Disclosures: Powers became Dean on Sept 1, 2000 (faculty since 1977). Derrick served on the UT Law School Foundation board and resigned when Powers joined Enron's board. Enron pledged $250,000 to the Law School in 1998 (final payment Jan 2001) plus $2,250 in matching gifts, and V&E is a major Law School supporter. Winokur has been a director since 1985 and chaired the Finance Committee.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Committee engages Wilmer, Cutler & Pickering as counsel, which engages Deloitte & Touche for accounting help. Prior unrelated work for Enron by both firms is disclosed, including Deloitte's late-2001 peer review of Andersen.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron files a Form 8-K with more information on the charges and on LJM1/LJM2, and announces its intent to restate financials for 1997-2000 and Q1-Q2 2001.
Notes: Same filing as source S066.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron files its Form 10-Q with more information about the restatement.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron and certain subsidiaries file voluntary Chapter 11 petitions.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Counsel reviews more than 430,000 pages of documents and interviews more than 65 people: nine current directors, more than 50 current and former employees, and some outside advisors.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Fastow provides a limited number of documents and submits to a brief interview in which he declines to answer most questions. The Committee also has had little or no access to e-mails still being retrieved from archive tapes.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Andersen allows review of some but not all workpapers, provides no copies, and allows no interviews. The LJM partnerships decline to provide documents, citing confidentiality with limited partners.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: About 60% of Enron's 1996-98 earnings came from businesses it was not in ten years earlier, and 30-40% from businesses it was not in five years earlier. Heavy capital investment pressured the balance sheet, and investment-grade ratings were vital to trading.
Direct_Quote: Maintaining Enron's credit ratings at investment grade was vital to the conduct of its energy trading business.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron Management preferred off-balance-sheet treatment to look better on analyst and rating-agency ratios. It used SPEs widely, including synthetic leases (e.g., its Houston headquarters), sales of financial assets, and sales of Enron stock to merchant 'hedging' SPEs.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Chewco is apparently the first time Fastow's Finance group used an SPE run by an Enron employee to keep a significant partnership off the books. Its ownership was 'a mystery to most Enron employees.' Unlike LJM, the employee's participation was never presented to or approved by the Board.
Direct_Quote: Chewco's ownership structure was a mystery to most Enron employees

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Chewco's financing fell at least $6.6 million (more than 50%) short of required third-party equity, yet Enron treated it as unconsolidated from 1997 through March 2001.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: On close review in late October and early November 2001, Enron and Andersen conclude Chewco lacked sufficient outside equity and should have been consolidated. Chewco-specific restatement: net income -$28M (1997), -$133M (1998), -$153M (1999), -$91M (2000), and debt +$711M, +$561M, +$685M, +$628M.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron and CalPERS form JEDI: Enron contributes $250 million in Enron stock and CalPERS $250 million in cash.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron considers a $1 billion 'JEDI II' partnership with CalPERS and proposes to buy out CalPERS' JEDI interest. CalPERS retains an investment bank to value it.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Fastow initially proposes that he manage and invest in a new entity, 'Chewco Investments,' named after the Star Wars character Chewbacca, with most equity from third parties.
Direct_Quote: named after the Star Wars character 'Chewbacca.'

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Fastow tells employees that Skilling had approved his participation in Chewco as long as it would not have to be disclosed in the proxy statement.
Direct_Quote: Skilling ... had approved his participation in Chewco as long as it would not have to be disclosed in Enron's proxy statement.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Skilling recalls Fastow proposing that Chewco's outside investors be members of Fastow's wife's family, and says he told Fastow he did not think that was a good idea.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Counsel advises that Fastow's participation would require proxy disclosure and Chairman/CEO approval under the Code of Conduct. As a result Kopper, not a senior officer, is substituted as manager, so no proxy disclosure is required (Code approval still is).

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Enron; CalPERS; Michael Kopper; Vinson & Elkins
Description: Enron agrees to redeem CalPERS' JEDI interest for $383 million. Chewco is formed as a Delaware LLC on very short notice, with Kopper (through intermediaries) the sole member. V&E drafts the documents in about 48 hours.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: A bridge facility lets Chewco borrow $383 million unsecured from two banks, guaranteed by Enron. Employees understood the structure did not comply with SPE rules (Kopper controlled it, and there was no third-party equity) and planned to fix it by year-end.
Direct_Quote: Enron employees involved in the transaction understood that the Chewco structure did not comply with SPE consolidation rules.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: During the JEDI waterfall negotiations with Kopper, Fastow tells Enron's negotiator (who reported to him) that he is pushing too hard for Enron and the deal needs to close, and says he is comfortable closing on Kopper's terms. The negotiator is uncomfortable and believes Enron could have done better.
Direct_Quote: suggested that he was pushing too hard for Enron and that the deal needed to be closed.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Enron Board Executive Committee; Jeffrey Skilling; Andrew Fastow
Description: By conference call, Skilling presents the JEDI background and Fastow describes Chewco as an SPE 'not affiliated with either Enron or CalPERS,' with financing of a $250M Enron-guaranteed loan, a $132M JEDI advance and $11M 'equity' (source unstated). The Committee approves Enron's guaranties. Lay joined during Fastow's presentation, and Kopper was on the call, but his role was not mentioned.
Direct_Quote: reviewed the economics of the project, the financing arrangements, and the corporate structure of the acquiring company.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Executive Committee briefly reports the Chewco guaranty approvals to the full Board.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Lay says he does not know Kopper and is confident he was never informed of or asked to approve Kopper's Chewco role.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Skilling says he approved Kopper's Chewco role on Fastow's recommendation and believes he told the Board. No written record exists, and other directors, including Lay and John Duncan, do not recall it.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Other_Parties_or_Subject: Chewco; Big River Funding LLC; Little River Funding LLC
Description: To address the control issue, Chewco is converted to a limited partnership with Kopper managing its general partner, and Big River Funding LLC (sole member Little River Funding LLC) becomes its limited partner.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Kopper assigns his ownership interest in Big River and Little River to William D. Dodson, leaving him no formal interest in Chewco's limited partner. The Report notes it is now common knowledge that Kopper and Dodson are domestic partners.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Enron; Michael Kopper; Barclays Bank PLC; JEDI
Description: New Chewco capital structure: $240M unsecured subordinated Barclays loan (Enron-guaranteed), $132M JEDI revolver advance, and $11.5M 'equity' (~3%). Kopper invests ~$115,000 in the GP and ~$10,000 in the LP (later transferred to Dodson). No third-party investors are found despite a private placement memorandum.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Barclays provides $11.4 million of 'equity loans' documented as 'certificates' and 'funding agreements' paying 'yield,' so Barclays can treat them as loans and Enron/Chewco as equity. Barclays requires $6.6 million of cash reserve accounts at closing, fully pledged to secure repayment.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Other_Parties_or_Subject: Coda Energy, Inc.; Taurus Energy Corp.
Description: JEDI sells its interest in Coda Energy (and subsidiary Taurus). Chewco's share of the proceeds is $16.6 million, distributed specially to fund the reserves. Employees say the sale was unrelated to the Chewco buyout.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Enron officer; Michael Kopper; Vinson & Elkins
Description: A letter agreement drafted by V&E and signed by an Enron officer and Kopper lets Chewco use $6,580,000 to fund reserve accounts (Little River $197,400; Big River $6,382,600). At closing JEDI wires $6.6 million to Barclays.
Direct_Quote: fund ... reserve accounts in an aggregate amount equal to $6,580,000

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The cash collateral was 'fatal' to Chewco's 3% compliance, so Chewco and JEDI should have been consolidated from November 1997. Many participants, including the officer who signed the letter and wire, claim no recollection, but others say it was openly discussed, and contemporaneous evidence supports them. Kopper clearly knew.
Direct_Quote: The existence of this cash collateral for the Barclays funding was fatal to Chewco's compliance with the 3% equity requirement.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Glisan attended meetings where the reserves were discussed. A handwritten note apparently by him lists a 'unique characteristic' of Chewco as 'minimization of 3% party capital.' He declined to explain.
Direct_Quote: minimization of 3% party capital

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Andersen bills $80,000 for its 1997 review of Chewco.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Andersen's CEO testifies that the firm performed 'audit procedures' in 1997, knew $11.4 million came from 'a large international financial institution,' and concluded 3% was met, but was unaware of the cash collateral. Workpapers show Andersen knew of the $16.6M distribution.
Direct_Quote: audit procedures ... a large international financial institution
Notes: CEO's name is not in this passage; supplied from public record.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Kopper, via the Chewco GP, is paid about $2 million in fees with no clear justification, including a $500,000/yr 'management fee' to SONR #1 (Kopper over 95%, Dodson the rest), totaling $1.6M through Dec 2000 and drawn mainly from the JEDI revolver.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Chewco's back-office work was done by an Enron employee on Enron time and, at times, apparently by Fastow's wife, a former Enron Finance employee.
Notes: Wife's name not given in this passage.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron pays Chewco $400,000, variously called a 'restructuring,' 'amendment' or 'nuisance' fee, with no identifiable basis. Glisan signs the wire approval.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: On repurchasing Chewco's JEDI interest, Enron lets Chewco extend repayment on $15 million of the revolver, unsecured and non-recourse.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Chewco agrees to pay Enron a $10 million guaranty fee for the $240M Barclays loan guaranty, among steps beginning December 1997 to accelerate revenue recognition from JEDI.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The guaranty fee ($10M up front plus 315 bp a year) was set by deal economics and accelerated revenue goals, not risk. Chewco pays Enron $17.4M over 12 months, sourced from JEDI. Enron books the $10M as a 'structuring fee' in December 1997, inconsistent with rules requiring recognition over the guaranty period.
Direct_Quote: These were not in fact 'structuring fees'

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron and Chewco amend the JEDI agreement to convert 80% of Enron's annual management fee into a 'required payment.' As of March 31, 1998, Enron records a $28M asset and recognizes $25.7M of income immediately. Glisan reportedly suggested the change to boost Q1 1998 earnings, and the accounting appears incorrect if services had not yet been rendered.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron records income from appreciation of its own stock held by JEDI, under a formula developed with Andersen in 1996, despite GAAP generally prohibiting it. Andersen workpapers show $126M recorded in Q1 2000.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron stock held by JEDI falls about $94M. Enron does not record its ~$90M share after Andersen reportedly says that since gains were not being recorded, losses should not be. The Committee cannot reconcile this with prior years' gains.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Senior Enron Finance personnel; Andrew Fastow
Description: Finance personnel conclude JEDI is in liquidation mode and an expensive off-balance-sheet vehicle. Fastow agrees, and buyout planning begins.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Jeffrey McMahon (SVP Finance & Treasurer); Andrew Fastow; Michael Kopper
Description: McMahon proposes a buyout giving Chewco investors a $1M return (152% IRR, 7.99x). Fastow reports back that he negotiated $10M and says Skilling approved it. A handwritten memo to 'Andy' (in Kopper's hand) references $10.5M. McMahon says $10M would be inappropriate.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Fastow tells the Committee he did not participate in the Chewco buyout talks because Kopper was his LJM2 partner. Several witnesses and the 'Andy' memo contradict this, and Fastow declines to answer questions about the memo.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: By mid-2000 Enron decides to buy Chewco's interest for a $10.5M return to investors ($7.5M already received plus $3M at closing). Skilling denies any involvement.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron and Chewco sign a Purchase Agreement at a $35M contract price: $3M cash plus $5.7M of 'required payments' plus $26.3M toward the revolver. At closing Enron keeps $5.7M and wires $29.3M; Chewco pays down $26.3M and keeps $3M. The remaining $15M becomes a term loan due Jan 2003, tied undisclosed to Osprey Trust certificates.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The $5.7M was labeled 'breakage costs.' Some evidence suggests the generic label was used because it was less likely to draw Andersen's attention. Enron paid Andersen $25,000 for the buyout review.
Direct_Quote: There is some evidence that this generic description was used because it was less likely to draw attention from Andersen

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Kopper and Dodson receive about $7.5M net cash plus $3M at closing on $125,000, an IRR above 360%, excluding $1.6M of management fees and a tax-free buyout.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron pays Chewco $2.6M under the 1997 Tax Indemnity Agreement. There is credible evidence Fastow authorized it even though in-house counsel unequivocally said there was no basis.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Michael Kopper; Enron in-house counsel; Vinson & Elkins
Description: Kopper requests a tax indemnity payment for the buyout. In-house counsel and V&E conclude the agreement does not cover it and tell Kopper so. Kopper says he will consult Fastow, and Fastow calls counsel, who tells him unequivocally that nothing is owed.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Fastow tells counsel he spoke with Skilling, who 'had decided that the payment should be made.' Enron pays $2.6M in September 2001. Skilling does not recall this, and Fastow declines to respond.
Direct_Quote: Skilling ... had decided that the payment should be made.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Responding to media reports, the Board requests a Chewco briefing, which Glisan gives on short notice. A follow-up review by accounting, legal and V&E finds the reserve-account documents, which Enron shows to Andersen.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: After reviewing the documents, Andersen provides a notice of 'possible illegal acts,' later highlighted in its CEO's December 12, 2001 testimony.
Direct_Quote: possible illegal acts

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Shown the $6.6M collateral evidence, Glisan agrees it precludes any argument that Chewco met 3%, but says he was unaware of it at the time.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron announces it will restate to consolidate Chewco and JEDI as of November 1997.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The LJM partnerships 'rarely lost money' on closed deals with Enron, even when assets declined, producing substantial income recognition and loss avoidance for Enron.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Fastow discusses with Lay and Skilling a partnership (LJM Cayman, LP) with himself as GP, presented as something he did not personally desire but needed to attract investors for the Rhythms hedge. Lay and Skilling agree to take it to the Board.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Enron Board; Kenneth Lay; Jeffrey Skilling; Andrew Fastow
Description: Lay calls on Skilling, who calls on Fastow. Fastow describes LJM1 and the hedge, discloses he will be GP, says he will invest $1M and receive management fees, and says Code action is needed. The Board approves and ratifies the Office of the Chairman's determination that his participation 'will not adversely affect the interests' of Enron.
Direct_Quote: will not adversely affect the interests

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Other_Parties_or_Subject: ERNB Ltd. (CSFB affiliate); Campsie Ltd. (NatWest affiliate)
Description: LJM1 is formed. Fastow is sole managing member of LJM Partners, LLC, and raises $15M from two limited partners. The Board was told Enron-stock appreciation would go only to limited partners, and Fastow would get 100% of other proceeds up to a 25% return, then half.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: LJM1 does three deals with Enron: the Rhythms hedge, the purchase of part of Enron's Cuiaba (Brazil) power project interest, and Osprey Trust certificates.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Andrew Fastow; Finance Committee (Lay, Skilling attending)
Description: Fastow proposes LJM2, a fund of $200M or more to buy assets Enron wants to syndicate. As controls, all deals are to be approved by Causey and Buy with annual Audit Committee review. The Committee recommends a finding that his participation won't adversely affect Enron.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Herbert Winokur (Finance Committee Chair); Enron Board
Description: Winokur presents the recommendation and controls. The Board unanimously 'adopt[s] and ratif[ies]' the Office of the Chairman's determination permitting Fastow to form LJM2.
Direct_Quote: adopt[ing] and ratify[ing]

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: LJM2's Private Placement Memorandum touts an 'unusually attractive investment opportunity' from its Enron link. It names Fastow, Kopper and Glisan as managers, says Enron will be its 'primary source of investment opportunities,' and says Fastow's 'access to Enron's information ... will contribute to superior returns.' Enron lawyers and V&E reviewed drafts only to ensure the solicitation did not appear to come from Enron.
Direct_Quote: access to Enron's information pertaining to potential investments will contribute to superior returns.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Other_Parties_or_Subject: ~50 limited partners incl. American Home Assurance, Arkansas Teachers Retirement System, MacArthur Foundation, Merrill Lynch, J.P. Morgan, Citicorp, First Union, Deutsche Bank, GE Capital, Dresdner Kleinwort Benson
Description: LJM2 has about 50 limited partners with aggregate commitments of $394M. Fastow is managing member of the GP's GP, and Kopper manages limited partner Big Doe LLC.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Kopper resigns from Enron and buys Fastow's interest in LJM2. Kopper had certified Code compliance in writing as recently as September 2000 without obtaining the required consent.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron agrees to have its staff perform 'purely ministerial' tasks for LJM at market rates. In the same month, Causey and Fastow sign an agreement letting Enron employees work for LJM, with LJM paying bonuses and some salaries.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: A second Services Agreement memorializes the arrangement, acknowledging that some LJM2 employee work 'will also be for the benefit of Enron.' What LJM2 actually paid is unknown.
Direct_Quote: some activities conducted by LJM2 employees will also be for the benefit of Enron

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Andersen workpapers note June 2000 changes strengthening LJM2 limited partners' rights to remove the GP. The Committee finds no clear answer on whether consolidation was required.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron invests $10M in Rhythms: 5.4M shares at $1.85.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Rhythms goes public at $21 and closes its first day at $69. By May 1999 Enron's stake is worth ~$300M but is locked up through year-end.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Jeffrey Skilling; Andrew Fastow; Ben Glisan
Description: Skilling, concerned about Rhythms volatility, wants to hedge it, which is commercially impossible. Fastow and Glisan devise a plan to use 'trapped' value in Enron-stock forward contracts to capitalize an SPE that would hedge Rhythms.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Fastow tells the Board that Enron-stock value will move to LJM1 for a note, that he will not receive 'any current or future (appreciated) value of ENE stock,' and that an outside firm will give a fairness opinion.
Direct_Quote: any current or future (appreciated) value of ENE stock

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Enron; LJM1; LJM Swap Sub L.P.
Description: The Rhythms transaction closes. Enron transfers 3.4M restricted Enron shares (~$276M; discounted ~$108M/39% for a four-year restriction) to LJM1 for a $64M note. LJM1 gives Swap Sub 1.6M shares and $3.75M cash, and Swap Sub gives Enron a put on 5.4M Rhythms shares at $56 (June 2004), valued at ~$104M.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: PwC opines that the Enron shares were worth $170-223M and the put plus note $164-204M, so the consideration was fair to Enron.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The deal terms are adjusted (shorter put, larger note) without explanation. There is no evidence the changes were presented to Lay and Skilling as the Board resolution required.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: At formation, Swap Sub had negative equity (a $104M put liability vs. $3.75M cash plus $80M restricted stock), raising a substantial question about 3% compliance.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Andersen's CEO testifies that in October 2001 the firm determined its 'initial judgment that the 3 percent test was met was in error' and 'promptly told Enron to correct it.'
Direct_Quote: When we reviewed this transaction again in October 2001, we determined that our team's initial judgment that the 3 percent test was met was in error. We promptly told Enron to correct it.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Kaminski says he strongly recommended to Buy that Enron not proceed, citing Fastow's conflict, a payout skewed against Enron, and instability from Enron-stock capitalization. Buy recalls no such discussions.
Direct_Quote: the transaction involved an obvious conflict of interest because of Fastow's personal involvement

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron enters four more no-cost Rhythms options with Swap Sub to bring the hedge closer to a swap, modeled by Kaminski's analysts for Glisan.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: LJM1 repays the $64M note plus interest three months early. The source is unclear: possibly new capital or sales of restricted Enron stock (Enron volume that day was 5.1M shares, about twice normal). Glisan's 'FY 99 Accomplishments' credits 'LJM1 Liquidity.'
Direct_Quote: LJM1 Liquidity—Transaction resulted in additional partnership capital being invested into LJM so that an [sic] $64 MM loan from ENE could be repaid.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: LJM1 buys an interest in the Cuiaba project from Enron for $11.3M.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Skilling decides to liquidate the Rhythms position (lock-up expired, price declined, volatility continuing).

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Kaminski's group finds a 68% probability that the Rhythms structure would default. Accounting says it suspected as much. Causey recalls credit-risk discussions but not the figure, and no reserve is found.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Causey approaches Fastow to unwind. Fastow says he has no interest in the Enron stock and is negotiating with his limited partners, then proposes that Swap Sub receive $30M. Causey's team deems it fair.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron gives Swap Sub, for no premium, a put on 3.1M Enron shares at $71.31 when the stock closed at $67.19, about $12.8M in the money.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Richard Causey (Enron); Andrew Fastow (Swap Sub; 'Southampton, L.P.')
Description: A letter agreement sets the unwind: options terminated, Swap Sub returns 3.1M Enron shares but keeps $3.75M, and Enron pays $16.7M. Enron also lends Swap Sub $10M so Fastow can buy out an LJM1 limited partner. Final agreement effective April 28, 2000.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Enron Board; Kenneth Lay; Jeffrey Skilling
Description: No fairness opinion, no Board notice and no DASH for the unwind. Lay was unaware, and Skilling knew of the sale but not the terms.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron gives up $207M of Rhythms options plus $27M cash for restricted shares it values at $234M unrestricted. Properly discounted, they were worth ~$161M, so Enron overpaid by more than $70M. LJM1 also kept 3.6M shares worth $251M undiscounted.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Andrew Fastow; Michael Kopper; Ben Glisan; Kristina Mordaunt; Kathy Lynn; Anne Yaeger Patel
Description: 'Unbeknownst to virtually everyone at Enron,' these six obtain financial interests in the Rhythms unwind in March 2000. Fastow's participation contradicts his Board representation that he would get no Enron stock value. None obtained Code approval, all had certified compliance in writing, and all were working on Enron–LJM2 deals.
Direct_Quote: Unbeknownst to virtually everyone at Enron, several Enron employees had obtained, in March 2000, financial interests in the unwind transaction.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Big Doe LLC (Kopper signing); Fastow Family Foundation (Fastow as 'Director'); Glisan; Mordaunt; Lynn; Yaeger Patel; Michael Hinds (LJM2 employee)
Description: The Southampton Place partnership agreement is signed to buy part of an existing LJM1 limited partner's interest. Contributions: Big Doe $25,000; Fastow Foundation $25,000; Glisan and Mordaunt $5,800 each; others less, for a $70,000 total.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Kopper approaches Mordaunt, saying LJM1 limited-partner managers want to sell part of their interest and assuring her LJM1 is doing no new business with Enron. Fastow makes a similar pitch to Glisan.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Counsel says her 'superiors' told her she would get a 'bonus' for LJM work, paid by letting LJM employees buy small Southampton interests, and that 'internal company counsel advising LJM' told her all approvals had been obtained.
Direct_Quote: bonus

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Glisan asks LJM1's counsel whether the investment is an Enron related-party transaction and is told it is not. Neither consults Enron's counsel. Mordaunt says she believed LJM1 was not doing business with Enron and, in hindsight, did not consider it carefully enough.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: There is some evidence Chewco transferred $1 million to LJM1 limited partner Campsie around the Rhythms unwind.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Amid media attention, Mordaunt voluntarily discloses her Southampton investment to Enron.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Fastow Family Foundation receives $4.5 million on its $25,000. Glisan and Mordaunt each say they received about $1 million on $5,800 within one or two months. Kopper gave Mordaunt no explanation beyond Enron wanting to end the options early.
Notes: OCR reads '$7 million' (likely '$1 million', matching p.290).

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Glisan succeeds McMahon as Treasurer. In 2000 he presents Raptor I to the Board and is listed as 'business unit originator' and 'person negotiating for Enron' on Raptor I, II and IV, signing each approval. He says Fastow never asked for favors.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Mordaunt is Enron's business-unit counsel on the Backbone dark-fiber sale to LJM2 and signs its approval sheet.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Michael Kopper (MD); Kathy Lynn (VP); Anne Yaeger Patel
Description: All three are named in the Enron–LJM2 Services Agreement as doing LJM2 work in 2000 and being paid by both Enron and LJM2.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Facing a possible $500M Q1 2001 impairment, Management restructures the Raptors without Board notice. In Q3 2001 it terminates them, taking a $544M after-tax ($710M pre-tax) charge plus a $1.2B equity cut ($1B for errors on stock issued to Raptors in Q2 2000 and Q1 2001, and $200M from termination).
Direct_Quote: Without bringing this issue to the attention of the Board, and with the design and effect of avoiding a massive credit reserve, Enron Management restructured the vehicles

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Raptors let Enron avoid almost $1B of merchant losses. Excluding $1.1B of Raptor income, pre-tax earnings of $1.5B would have been $429M, a 72% decline.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: At Skilling's urging, staff begin devising a way to hedge the merchant portfolio. Skilling wants to protect values and avoid quarterly volatility.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Enron (via Harrier); LJM2; Ben Glisan (lead); Andersen; Vinson & Elkins
Description: Raptor I (Talon LLC) is created. LJM2 invests $30M. Enron's Harrier contributes $1,000, a $50M note, and Enron stock and contracts worth ~$537M, discounted ~35% for a three-year restriction (PwC fairness opinion). Enron receives a $400M note. Andersen billed ~$335,000 for creating the Raptors.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: An unwritten understanding (not in documents or Board materials) bars Talon from hedging until LJM2 receives $41M or 30% annualized, whichever is greater. LJM2 can put its interest to Enron if not paid in six months. The terms were 'remarkably favorable to LJM2' and 'served no apparent business purpose for Enron,' and LJM2 bore no first-dollar risk.
Direct_Quote: These terms were remarkably favorable to LJM2, and served no apparent business purpose for Enron.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Fastow tells LJM2 investors the Raptors were 'divested investments' after the $41M return, and in April 2001 that 'LJM2 had already received its return of and on capital.'
Direct_Quote: LJM2 had already received its return of and on capital.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron buys from Talon, for a $41M premium, a put on ~7.2M Enron shares at $57.50 (stock at $68), expiring Oct 18, 2000. This was effectively a bet against its own stock and priced as if Talon were creditworthy.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: At Fastow's suggestion, the put is settled early. Talon returns $4M to Enron but pays LJM2 $41M, which LJM2 reports as a 193% annualized return. Enron also pays LJM2's fees and $250,000 a year.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Ben Glisan; Richard Causey; Richard Buy; Scott Sefton
Description: Weeks after closing, Glisan, Causey and Buy sign the LJM2 Approval Sheet (Skilling's line blank), which names Kopper (an Enron MD) as LJM2's negotiator. The Deal Summary, signed by Glisan and Sefton, projects a 76.8% annualized LJM2 return.
Direct_Quote: It is expected that Talon will have earnings and cash sufficient to distribute $41 million to LJM2 within six months, yielding an annualized return on investment to LJM2 of 76.8%

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Ben Glisan; Richard Causey (Lay, Skilling, Fastow present)
Description: Glisan presents Raptor as 'a risk management program' with $400M of 'excess' stock giving ~$200M P&L protection and LJM2 getting 30% plus fees (the $41M floor is not disclosed). The Corporate Secretary's notes read 'Does not transfer economic risk but transfers P&L volatility.' Causey says Andersen was 'comfortable,' and listed risks include 'accounting scrutiny.'
Direct_Quote: Does not transfer economic risk but transfers P&L volatility.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: A Raptor presentation for EBS states it is '[n]ot an economic hedge; ... credit risk retained with Enron Corp.'
Direct_Quote: Not an economic hedge; ... credit risk retained with Enron Corp.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Board approves Project Raptor the day after the Finance Committee recommends it.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Talon–Enron total return swaps (~$734M notional) are agreed in mid-September but backdated 'as of' August 3, 2000, the day Avici stock hit its all-time high of $162.50. By quarter-end Avici was $95, so the backdating let Enron offset nearly $75M of losses.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Zisman writes that most investments put into Raptor are 'bad ones' and that this 'might lead one to believe that the financial books at Enron are being "cooked".' He later tells senior attorneys he didn't know whether only bad assets were chosen. Recipients believe the memo untrue and take no further action.
Direct_Quote: As it turns out, we have discovered that a majority of the investments being introduced into the Raptor Structure are bad ones. ... it might lead one to believe that the financial books at Enron are being 'cooked' in order to eliminate a drag on earnings

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron puts a 'costless collar' on ~7.6M Enron shares in Talon (floor $81, ceiling $116), effectively lifting the restriction that justified the 35% ($187M) discount. Causey signs the waiver.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Executive Committee authorizes Raptor II after Fastow says 'there had been tremendous utilization by the business units of Raptor I.' In fact Talon had done no derivatives with Enron yet. Closing documents are dated June 29, 2000.
Direct_Quote: there had been tremendous utilization by the business units of Raptor I

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron sells rights to 18M contingent Enron shares for 2003 delivery: Raptor I 3.9M, II 7.8M, IV 6.3M, contingent on the March 1, 2003 stock price.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Ben Glisan; Jeffrey Skilling; Enron Board
Description: Glisan says Raptor I is 'almost completely utilized' and Raptor II not available until later, without explaining the LJM2 return condition, and proposes another Raptor. Skilling reports Raptor II to the Board, which approves Raptor IV. Closing documents are dated Sept 11, 2000.
Direct_Quote: Raptor I was almost completely utilized

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron pays Timberwolf and Bobcat $41M each for puts, settled early, with ~$41M each distributed to LJM2. Derivatives totaling $513M notional are done with Timberwolf only.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Causey approves collars on Timberwolf (floor $79, cap $112) and Bobcat (floor $83, cap $112) shares, contradicting the restriction discounts.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Jeffrey Skilling; Richard Buy; Richard Causey
Description: Skilling signs the LJM2 Approval Sheet for Raptor IV, his only Raptor sheet. It is signed in March 2001, six months after closing.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Other_Parties_or_Subject: LJM2 and other investors; The New Power Company (TNPC)
Description: Enron (75% owner of TNPC) sells TNPC warrants to investors including LJM2 at $10.75 per share. Earlier it sold holdings to Hawaii 125-0 and kept risk via total return swaps.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Raptor III is created with Enron contributing ~24M TNPC shares (warrants) at $10.75 for a $259M note recorded at zero. It is not presented to the Board, with no approval sheet, DASH or fairness opinion. LJM2 invests $30M.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Five days before the Porcupine transfer at $10.75, Enron offers employees TNPC IPO shares, noting 'the current estimated price range ... is $18.00 to $20.00 per share.'
Direct_Quote: the current estimated price range [for the shares] is $18.00 to $20.00 per share.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: TNPC IPOs at $21 and closes at $27. Porcupine distributes $39.5M to LJM2 (an internal rate of return LJM2 puts at 2500%), and Enron immediately swaps 18M TNPC shares at $21, locking in a ~$370M accounting gain.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: TNPC falls below its IPO price within a week and below $10 by mid-November, a 'double-whammy' for Porcupine.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: With derivatives over $1.5B notional, the daily tracking report shows Enron net gain (Raptor loss) slightly over $500M. Raptor I has negative credit capacity by mid-December.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: A 45-day cross-guarantee merges the four Raptors' credit capacity so no year-end reserve is needed. Enron pays LJM2 $50,000, and the Board is not informed. Andersen's Dec 28, 2000 memo approved it, but an amended Oct 12, 2001 version says Chicago partners advised it was not permissible.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Raptors' credit shortfall grows to $504M by quarter-end. Enron does not take the charge, does not tell the Board, and restructures instead.
Direct_Quote: Enron did not take this charge, and the Board was not informed of the situation.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Witnesses say Skilling called fixing the Raptors one of the Company's 'highest priorities' and personally thanked an accountant afterward. Skilling says he was told only generally, saw it as an accounting issue, and believes a loss could have been absorbed.
Direct_Quote: fixing the Raptors' credit capacity problem was one of the Company's highest priorities

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The restructuring is effective as of March 26, 2001 (documents dated April 13, after quarter-end, with a March 30 letter agreement). It cross-collateralizes the Raptors, has Enron agree to deliver up to 18M extra shares (notes +$260M), and sells Raptors II and IV 12M shares for 2005 at $47 (a 23% discount; notes +$568M) while also collaring them. Enron books only a $36.6M reserve instead of $504M.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Kaminski learns the discounted shares were simultaneously collared and tells Andersen and the accountants this cannot be reconciled with the 23% discount.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: They realize Enron wrongly booked notes for stock sold to Raptors as equity increases: $172M (Talon, Q2-Q4 2000) and $828M (Timberwolf/Bobcat, Q1-Q2 2001).

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: They conclude the entries were wrong and decide to correct them in Q3 2001 as 'not material' without restatement. The $1.2B equity cut equals the $1B correction plus $200M ($2.1B of stock returned vs. $1.9B of notes).

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Richard Causey; Kenneth Lay (CEO again); Greg Whalley (COO)
Description: Causey presents options on the Raptors (keep, ameliorate, terminate), and Lay and Whalley direct him to terminate them.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Enron (Fastow negotiating for Enron); LJM2 (Kopper negotiating)
Description: Enron terminates the Raptors and pays LJM2 about $35M, privately negotiated between Fastow (who had sold his LJM2 interest in July) and Kopper and based on a $61M residual interest. Raptor assets were ~$2.5B (Enron stock at a restricted $2.1B, as Andersen insisted) vs. liabilities of ~$3.2B, and Enron stock was $27.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Andersen tells Enron to charge the excess to income rather than goodwill, resulting in a ~$710M pre-tax ($544M after-tax) charge. Enron had booked $532M (2000) plus $545M (9M 2001) of Raptor earnings, still netting $367M. The Committee suggests the full $1.1B arguably should have been reversed.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Fastow reports LJM2 IRRs of 193%, 278%, 2500% and a projected 125% on the four Raptors, far above the 30% told to the Finance Committee.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Committee concludes LJM2's returns were 'for a service provided: LJM2 lent its name to a vehicle by which Enron could circumvent accounting convention.' Losses were moved from income to equity, and 'Enron was hedging with itself.' Andersen Chicago national-office experts were involved.
Direct_Quote: LJM2 lent its name to a vehicle by which Enron could circumvent accounting convention.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Fastow privately tells LJM2 investors that their return 'was not at risk' because LJM2 'had already received its return of and on capital,' especially for Raptor III. This undercuts the 3% equity-at-risk requirement.
Direct_Quote: LJM2's return on these investments was not at risk to the performance of derivatives in the vehicles, given that LJM2 had already received its return of and on capital.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: The Committee lists seven accounting problems: own-stock gains, insufficient equity at risk, cost vs. equity method, use of restriction discounts, the $259M Porcupine note ignored (overstating capacity), collars as a possible dividend, and the restructuring not avoiding the $504M Q1 impairment.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Andersen's total Raptor-related bill is ~$1.3M. It advised 'at every step,' Enron followed the advice, and the workpapers omit key issues. Many inside Enron viewed the Raptors as 'a triumph of accounting ingenuity,' which the Committee calls mistaken.
Direct_Quote: a triumph of accounting ingenuity

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Pre-tax earnings, reported vs. without Raptors ($M): 3Q00 364 vs 295 (+69); 4Q00 286 vs -176 (+462); 1Q01 536 vs 281 (+255); 2Q01 530 vs 490 (+40); 3Q01 -219 vs -461 (+251, excluding the $710M charge). Total 1,506 vs 429 (+1,077).

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: There were almost 20 other transactions from September 1999 to July 2001. Of seven assets sold in 2H 1999, five were repurchased, LJM profited on all, and there is some evidence of undocumented side deals insuring LJM against loss in three.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Other_Parties_or_Subject: LJM1; EPE (Empresa Productora de Energia Ltda)
Description: Enron sells LJM1 a 13% EPE (Cuiaba, Brazil power plant) stake for ~$11.3M, deconsolidating EPE and booking $34M (Q3) plus $31M (Q4) of mark-to-market income on a gas contract. Glisan (reporting to Fastow) told the seller in June 1999 that LJM1 would buy, and roles were confused.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record

Skilling cites misrepresentations to LJM1, while a Fastow subordinate says Fastow told her there was a clear understanding Enron would buy it back.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record

Description: ENA pools loans into a CLO trust and sells ~$324M of notes and equity. The unsellable lowest tranches go to a Whitewing affiliate and LJM2, with LJM2 paying $32.5M ($12.9M for equity). The ENA finance head reportedly tells a Whitewing investor Enron would make it whole.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Whitewing affiliate (signed by an Enron employee)
Description: Two days before its CLO purchase, a Whitewing affiliate lends LJM2 $38.5M. The signer does not recall it.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron gives the defaulting CLO trust a free $113M put. Much of its risk was 'hedged' in Raptor I effective Aug 3, 2000, before the put existed.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron repurchases all CLO notes at par plus interest and LJM2's equity at cost to protect its reputation.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron sells LJM2 75% of the Polish Nowa Sarzyna plant company for $30M and books a ~$16M gain. A lender waiver is valid only through March 31, 2000.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron and Whitewing buy out LJM2 for $31.9M, about a 25% return.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron sells LJM2 a 90% interest in MEGS (Gulf of Mexico gathering system), with LJM2 paying $25.6M for a $23.2M note plus equity, to avoid year-end consolidation. Enron has 90 days to remarket, with a 25% cap.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron repurchases at LJM2's maximum return. McMahon initially declines to sign the DASH, writing: 'There were no economics run to demonstrate this investment makes sense.'
Direct_Quote: There were no economics run to demonstrate this investment makes sense. Therefore, we cannot opine on its marketability or ability to syndicate.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Enron and an investor each pay $37.5M for Yosemite certificates. In late December, Enron seeks to cut its holding from 50% to 10% to avoid 10-K footnote disclosure.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: LJM2 demands a fee of $1M or more, and Enron offers $100,000. Fastow calls the employee to complain he is negotiating too hard. McMahon confronts Fastow, LJM2 retreats, and the fee stays at $100,000.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Documents show sales on Dec 29 and 30, 1999, but the actual transaction occurs on February 28, 2000: Condor lends LJM2 $35M, LJM2 buys the certificates and passes them to Condor, and LJM2 earns $100,000 plus expenses. The approval sheet, prepared February 2000, says 'LJM2 intends to sell this investment to Condor within one week of purchase.'
Direct_Quote: LJM2 intends to sell this investment to Condor within one week of purchase.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Actor(s): Enron Broadband Services; LJM2 (Kopper, then Fastow)
Other_Parties_or_Subject: Kristina Mordaunt; Ken Rice; Richard Causey
Description: EBS decides to sell dark fiber by quarter-end to meet Q2 numbers. In late June, Fastow angrily complains to EBS GC Mordaunt (his Southampton partner) and lead negotiators about uncertified fiber. Causey and Rice sweeten terms (18% cap within two years, 25% after). Enron records a $54M gain, and this is the only LJM deal where Lay signed the DASH.

Source_Title: Powers Report (Enron board special investigation), House hearing record
Description: Other LJM deals: Osprey Trust ($15M, Sep 1999); Bob West Treasure ($3M, Dec 1999); Cortez ($0.7M, Jan 2000); Rawhide ($12.5M, Mar 2000); Blue Dog ($11.3M notional, May 2000); Margaux ($10M, Jun 2000); Coyote Springs ($42.9M notional, Jul 2000); TNPC warrants ($50M, Jul 2000); Osprey ($26M, Jul 2000); Osprey Associates ($6.5M, Oct 2000); Fishtail ($8M, Dec 2000; Enron recorded a $115M gain); JGB Trust/Avici ($1M, Dec 2000); LAB Trust/Catalytica ($1.8M, Dec 2000).
